comment: The public test, version, problem counts and official scoring are identified.
Rule inference, AI evaluation and intended comparisons are described.
Example grids, new inputs and required output grids are described.
Verified testing specifies settings, spending limits and permitted attempts.
Exact matching, within-problem fractions and averaging are explained.
Inferring new rules from examples is linked to the claimed reasoning ability.
Sources, human difficulty and duplicate-rule removal are justified; broader representativeness is unresolved.
Developer review, human solving and documented corrections show checks of puzzle materials and outputs.
The tasks cover grid-rule inference, with limited evidence for broader reasoning coverage.
Exact outputs demonstrate successful transformations, but scores alone do not establish the reasoning used.
Aggregation is explained, but its measurement justification is not supplied.
Public tests cover correct outputs, wrong dimensions, changed squares and missing outputs.
Human results and AI scores provide context, but the human study covered a larger puzzle pool.
The verified-testing policy explicitly uses one run.
No systematic study of changed instructions, presentation or software is supplied.
The reviewed materials provide no score-variation estimates or ranges.
Program-search resistance and repeated-rule checks address some possible shortcuts.
Hidden-data agreements and monitoring address exposure, but public-task exposure remains unresolved.
Development training is allowed, evaluation-specific adaptation discouraged and feedback-driven iteration restricted.
No supplied study links scores to other domains or real-world work.
Verified conditions are recorded; other testing routes differ, and human matching does not establish AI equivalence.
Public problems, running software and marking tests support inspection and repetition of public evaluations.
Public licensing and hidden-data confidentiality, handling and review rules are stated.
Dated corrections and code changes are recorded, but score effects are incompletely established.
Grid-task claims are supported; connections to broader intelligence exceed the supplied validation.
The original 2024 benchmark, question set and public scoring methods are identified.
Engineering-document abilities, evaluated AI systems and intended comparisons are described.
Inputs, six question groups and required answer formats are described.
Instructions and settings are described, but exact historical inputs and configurations are incompletely linked.
Text similarity, decision credit and equal weighting of task groups are explained.
The tasks are linked to activities involved in using engineering documents.
Practical sources support relevance, but one rulebook and uneven task coverage limit the rationale.
Additional reviewers checked manually written questions, with exceptions and limited explanation checks.
Six relevant activities are covered, but engineering domains and task proportions are narrow.
Correct decisions earn credit, but wording and incomplete references also affect marks.
Equal group weighting and distinct skill interpretations lack supplied validation.
Small marking-test files and examination of scoring problems demonstrate some testing.
Guessing and other AI results provide context; information supplies differ and no engineer baseline is reported.
Five passage configurations do not establish repetition under identical conditions.
Effects of passages, dimension labels, scale bars and image highlighting were examined.
Passage experiments provide some variation information, but main comparisons lack adequate uncertainty support.
Several unintended influences were examined, but shortcut testing remains incomplete.
Image novelty and possible exposure are discussed, without systematic overlap checks or an established protected set.
Clear training and repeated-submission policies were not available.
No supplied evidence establishes transfer to other technical documents or engineering projects.
Information supplies and setup effects are documented, but comparisons do not isolate AI ability consistently.
Public materials permit inspection, but incomplete historical records and an answer-file discrepancy limit reproduction.
A licence file and complete responsible-reuse rules were not found in the inspected material.
Code history identifies revisions, but their effects on scores are not clearly documented.
The paper acknowledges narrow coverage, imperfect marking and uncertain transfer to other documents.
The version, public test set and official scoring software are identified.
Rule inference, evaluated AI systems and comparison uses are described.
Example grids, new inputs and exact required outputs are described.
Verified evaluations specify settings, spending limits and permitted attempts; other routes may differ.
Exact input matching and averaging within and across problems are explained.
Inferring transformations from examples is explicitly linked to learning new rules.
Puzzle sources, human difficulty selection and duplicate-rule removal are explained; coverage of broader reasoning is not established.
Developer review and human solving informed selection, but explicit checking of all reference outputs is unclear; later corrections are documented.
Grid tasks support part of the reasoning claim, without evidence covering broader intelligence.
Exact outputs directly assess successful grid completion, but alternative routes to credit remain incompletely assessed.
The averaging rule is clear, but evidence supporting its interpretation as a combined ability measure is absent.
Public software tests cover correct grids, wrong sizes, changed squares and missing outputs; coverage is limited.
AI scores and human solving results provide context, but the human study pool exceeds the final set and testing routes differ.
The verified-testing policy explicitly uses one run; repetition for other reported evaluations is unclear.
No systematic study of changed instructions, presentation or software is supplied.
No score-variation estimates or ranges are supplied.
Design and review address program-search shortcuts and repeated rules, without comprehensive investigation.
Exposure monitoring and provider agreements address hidden-data risks, but public exposure and possible leakage remain unresolved.
Development training is allowed, evaluation-specific changes are discouraged and repeated feedback-driven improvement is restricted to preserve evaluation separation.
No supplied study connects scores to language, social interaction or real-world work.
Verified settings are recorded, but differing testing routes and limited AI comparability evidence remain.
Public tasks, software and marking tests support inspection; hidden materials and complete result records are not fully available or verified.
Public licensing and hidden-data confidentiality, provider-handling and code-review rules are stated.
Dated corrections and code changes are recorded, but their effects on all affected scores are not established.
Grid-performance claims have direct support; connections to broader intelligence exceed the supplied validation.
The original benchmark, question count, task groups and public scoring methods are identified.
Engineering document abilities, AI comparisons and broader intended interpretations are described.
Rules, drawings, images and required text or yes/no responses are described.
Instructions, settings and information routes are described, but historical inputs and settings are not fully linked to every result.
Marking methods and equal weighting of the six groups are explained.
Tasks are linked to finding, interpreting and applying engineering requirements in practical work.
Practical sources support relevance, but one rulebook and uneven task counts limit the selection's justification for broader use.
Additional reviewers checked manually written questions, with exceptions and narrower checks for some explanations.
Six groups cover several relevant activities, but one rulebook and a limited task range constrain coverage.
Correct decisions and relevant answers earn credit, but wording, formatting and incomplete references also affect marks.
Equal group weighting is described without evidence validating the combined score or distinct group abilities.
Small marking-test files and discussion of scoring problems establish some checking, without complete validation.
Random guessing and other AI systems provide comparisons, but information supplies differ and no engineer baseline is reported.
Five passage sets change the conditions and therefore do not establish identical-condition repeated testing.
Effects of changed passages, dimension labels, scale bars and highlighted images were examined.
Passage-set variation provides limited information, but uncertainty is insufficient for small differences in the main comparisons.
Formatting, retrieval and familiarity influences were examined; the always-yes opportunity is inferred rather than shown to have been tested.
Image novelty and possible exposure are discussed, but systematic overlap checks and protected evaluation data are not established.
Clear training and repeated-submission rules were not available in the reviewed sources.
No supplied evidence establishes transfer to other standards, documents or real engineering projects.
Information differences are described and some setup effects are tested, but comparisons do not isolate the AI from its information supply.
Public materials support inspection, but incomplete historical records and an answer-file discrepancy prevent complete reproduction.
A licence file and complete responsible-reuse rules were not found; this does not establish that reuse is prohibited.
Code history identifies revisions, but no clear record explains their effects on scores.
The paper acknowledges scope and marking limits, while broader competence claims and close rankings need further support.
